paragraphs.text: Yesterday's discourse on the body filled us with wonder. It set out the beauty of nature and marveled at the wisdom of the Architect. For when nature is explained, the Creator is glorified, and when the work is praised, honor goes to the craftsman. But while we were still occupied with this, the time for the evening service came upon us. While the speaker was preaching about the lamp of the body, the evening lamp was brought forward for the service of the church, and to that same lamp he added the remembrance of a third lamp, the lamp of the divine law. The first lamp, the lamp of the body, has testimony from the Life-giver himself: "The lamp of the body is the eye." The lamp made of fire is known to everyone from experience and daily use. The third lamp is proclaimed by David: "Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths." But today the teaching of our honored common father has shown us yet another lamp, the lamp of the gospel. This lamp does not rise against the sun but listens to the Sun of righteousness. Christ comes to be baptized, and John baptizes, not out of proud arrogance but in service to the divine command. A man who himself needed baptism baptized the One who baptizes all and is Lord of all. He did not come forward out of presumption but in obedience to the command. John is a lamp who bears in himself the pattern of the saints of the Old Testament. Just as the law of the Jews was called a lamp, so those who were virtuous according to the law were called lamps.

Pay attention, I beg you. John is a lamp, for the law and the prophets lasted until John. David is a lamp, for when in his old age he was eager to go out to war against Zabron, the elders of the people held him back and would not let him go to the war. They all raised the cry, "Do not go out to war, so that you do not quench the lamp of Israel." David is a lamp, and John is a lamp. But ever since the true Light dawned, the Sun of righteousness, and sent out its brilliant, clear rays from heaven, those who grow in virtue in that light far surpass the lamps. Those others shared the name of lamp because they served as soldiers under the law, which was called a lamp. But these, who are enlightened by the light of the gospel, who live by it and show the same form of life, have passed beyond the rank of lamp and are called light. Although a lamp is light, how can it compare with the original Light? What belonged to him by the order of nature, the King in his generosity granted to the disciples.

And see Christ's love for humankind. The name he gave himself he also let his disciples share. "I am," he says, "the light of the world"; and elsewhere, "You are the light of the world." O new graces and gifts, which go beyond every word and every thought! See how his love for humankind overcomes the order of nature. The sun rises. But why do I say that the sun rises? Even when it sends out its forerunner, the morning, from the east, it puts all the hosts of stars to flight, and all the stars hide and vanish. They are not destroyed; they are hidden by the greater light of the sun. But Jesus, the Sun of righteousness, who dawned after the first night, did more than make the prophets who shone out at his coming bright like stars. He also gathered other luminaries to himself. Luminaries rose with the Sun of righteousness: preachers of the truth, champions in the front line of godliness. Of them Paul says, "among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast the word of life, so that I may boast on the day of Christ."

Have you seen the rays of the Sun of righteousness? See also how the evangelist sets down names that rank above every name of the rhetoricians, above all vain philosophy, above grammarians and men of the arts, and above every honor and title of distinction [?]. What is there to say? Rustic names and heavenly minds accomplish very great things. Bartholomew and Thaddaeus are names foreign to the Greek tongue, yet they drive away all ignorance and plant all knowledge in its place. The Life-giver chose fishermen. He did not do this to disparage the wise or to dishonor the eloquent, but to keep the beginning of the preaching free from suspicion. The word is preached by fishermen so that the power of the One at work may be made plain. We do not marvel that they are fishermen; we marvel that the power that is above the world was proclaimed by fishermen.

God could have moved eloquent speakers to champion the preaching, so that the wisdom of the knowledge of God would be revealed. But he did not want to empty the truth of the cross. That is why Paul said, "I did not come with excellence of speech, so that the cross of Christ would not be made empty." That is, he did not want it to be thought something vain or be disparaged through words. Instead, the power of the Crucified planted the church through the band of apostles. He planted the word of truth through untrained tongues, which had been schooled only in the divine law, and after planting through them, he then waters through the wise as well. This was not done without reason. He did not want those who make excuses for their sins to say that he deceived the ignorant but could not persuade the wise and the powerful. So he did his skillful work through those whose minds seemed open to deception: fishermen, the simple, the unlearned and the incapable. For this reason, although not together with them, God raised up learned and eloquent preachers already in the time of the apostles. "A certain Jew named Apollos," it says, "an Alexandrian by birth, came to Ephesus. He was eloquent, mighty in the Scriptures and in understanding, and eloquent in interpretation." "Mighty," it says, "in the Scriptures." And what skill did he have? He was a great help to the believers. "In public," it says, "he refuted the Jews." Do you see how the sword of Christ is sharpened against everyone? He trains fishermen and he arms the wise. Since eloquence serves error, he often strips that weapon from wickedness and clothes virtue with it. Error has clothed itself in investigative arguments; truth seizes them and with those very arguments kills error. It is like blessed David when he brought down the giant Goliath. He first wounded him with his own weapons, and then he cut off his head with the foreigner's own sword: he took it from him and beheaded him with it. In the same way, truth knows how to draw the sword of error and kill error with it. There were wise men among the gentiles, and Christ sent zealous men from among the Jews to fight them as champions. Among the Jewish people there was a sword of steel, Saul, who in his error opposed the churches and was cutting the faith of Christ off at the root [?]. The Life-giver took that same sword and put it into the hands of the church, to drive away all evil that rises against it. This is what blessed David said: "Sinners drew the sword and strung their bows; their swords shall enter their own hearts, and their bows shall be broken."

God spoke through the wise, and he also spoke through the unlearned, so that he might show his power through both. He spoke through the fishermen so that their untrained tongues would disgrace the skill of vain words. He spoke through the wise so that their deep knowledge would expose cunning and, by surrounding the faith with a wall, make humanity secure. What he did with the unlearned and the eloquent, he also did with kings. Listen to how this was. At the beginning of the preaching, from the very first, the Life-giver could have brought kings to obey the preaching and raised them up as fellow soldiers for godliness, as they are now. But he did not do so. He did not want to bring the truth under suspicion, as if the church had been established by human protectors and not by the power of God. He stripped it of human help and clothed it with heavenly power. Until the most godly Constantine, thirty-five emperors of the Romans ruled one after another, and none of them was willing to submit in obedience to the faith. From this I learn that grace does not take any human [?] as its vessel but has its own power dwelling within it. He saw the whole world in error. Again he did not want those who make excuses for their sins to say that he could deceive the ignorant and unsuspecting but was unable to catch kings and princes in his snare. So he arms the word, brings kings under the yoke of godliness, and leads all the nations into one concord of truth. In this way it was made plain that the King of kings and Lord of lords showed the surpassing greatness of heavenly wisdom through humble preachers.

Today the names of the apostles were read. The fishermen were proclaimed, and the words of simple men were made famous, the words that offered the world all instruction. Mark the force of it: "The first of the twelve," it says, "was Simon, who was called Peter." He is the rock of the church and the foundation of godliness. He had the name Simon from his father and mother, and the name Peter from the Life-giver. "You are Peter," he says, which is translated "rock," "and on this rock I will build my church." All the preaching of the church stands firm on the rock, and every heretical error stands on crumbling clay. The firm rock that holds up the building is one thing, and the crumbling soil that gives its builders no steady ground is another. It cannot even hold itself steady. Their words crumble, their speech is cold, and their creeds deserve reproach, because human thoughts have been mixed into the faith of God. The clay tries to undermine the rock, but the rock is not given over to defeat: "The gates of hell," he says, "shall not prevail against it."

The disciples of the heretics are like potters who mold bricks. They mix straw into the soft clay to temper it, and so they make what is loose firmer, and what is rotten looks solid. It looks solid until something harmful comes against it. But if rain or flood or fire or anything else strikes it, it does not stand its ground [?]. For this reason the prophet speaks to those who trust in earthly things and think no harm will come from them: "Thus says the Lord: Go down into the clay, tread it with straw, make it harder than brick, and fire shall devour you." He rebukes those who trust in bodily and earthly things and think them a power that cannot be defeated. The foundation of the church is the rock; the foundation of the heretics is Jerusalem. The prophet wanted to show what kind of thing the church is, established on the rock, and what kind of thing the Jewish fold is, which has no standing and no firmness. Or rather, God himself wanted to show this through the prophet. He says to the prophet Ezekiel, "Take a brick, portray Jerusalem on it, and build a siege wall around it." Why a brick? So that you may learn the difference between the form of a brick and the form of a rock. Jerusalem stood on a brick, but the foundation of the church is the rock. Indeed, we also call the church a rock, and we are not lying; nor do I deny the rock on which it stands. The church is also a rock, because it has Christ as its firm rock. Another rock is Peter, who received the name through his confession: "You are," he says, "the Christ, the Son of the living God."

But I want to examine this closely. John the evangelist was full to overflowing. He gathered the rains of the gospel into himself; he was the son of thunder, who drew all the fullness of grace into himself at once. Why, then, did he not use Peter's words at the beginning of his Gospel? He did not say, "In the beginning was the Son," or "In the beginning was the Only-begotten." He set aside the titles "Son" and "Only-begotten" and came to "Word": "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Peter was called blessed not because he called him the Word but because he confessed him as the Son. Why, then, did blessed John leave aside the blessed confession and hurry to "Word"? The apostles knew what they were preaching, and they knew that some of those who would receive it could not bear the fullness of the words. The beginning of the preaching and its message sounded in worthy and unworthy ears alike. John did not want them, with merely human minds, to think of the divine teaching as involving passion. On hearing "Son," they would imagine a father and a mother, and gross matter, and the other needs of the body. Therefore he comes to the title "Word," which could explain from the very first words that he is beyond passion. And see what order he uses. He has set up a ladder, and by many steps he brings us up to the title "Son." He did not deny that title; he kept it for the fitting time.

"In the beginning," he says, "was the Word," so that you may learn that his birth was without passion and was free in its own proper way. For the mind is always the father of a word. "In the beginning," he says, "was the Word." A word would not even be called a word on its own if it were not someone's word. Whose, then, is the Word? "He was," he says, "in the beginning with God, and the Word was God." First he explains the birth that is without passion. Then, by showing that he is with the Father, he shows that he is inseparable from him and one with him in nature, in will and in operation. "And the Word was God": with this he states his honor a second time. It is clear that what is needed is not the reading of words but certainty about realities [?]. "In the beginning was the Word" makes plain the birth without passion. "And the Word was God [?]" makes plain the inseparable unity. "And God was the Word" makes plain the uncreated honor. "He was in the beginning with God": he repeats it to confirm the same meaning. He had called him "Word," but the words we use do not make the nature of what is spoken very clear. So he presents the Word more clearly and shows him to be God, Word and Creator all at once: "And all things were made through him."

Yet the heretics find a kind of remedy in this. "It says 'through him,'" they say, "not 'by him' or 'from him,' but 'through him.'" But I would truly like to learn from those who stumble. They do not know their own nature, yet they fall into such stumbling and search and probe that nature which surpasses every mind. What difference do they imagine between "through him" and "from him"? One must not give a verdict at random but must show proof from the holy Scriptures.

What does "through him" mean? "The Father," they say, "made things through him." They take refuge in this phrase and use it as a shelter for their wickedness, putting forward "the Father made through him." Tell me the manner of it, and do not just throw out the word in confusion. A word empty of meaning I cannot understand, for I am unlearned. When things are done "through" someone among us, we can understand the circumstances. A master works through a servant: one gives the command and the other carries it out. A master works through a craftsman: one sketches the design and the other carries out the work. Now tell me the manner. How does he work through the Son? Does he give commands like a master to a servant? Does he go like an unskilled man to a skilled one? Or does he finish the work like a craftsman with an axe or a saw or some other tool? Choose whatever example you like, but make clear what you understand, so that I may learn what I believe. Did he command like a master to a servant, or have a craftsman do the work like an unskilled man, or work with a tool like a craftsman? Come, tell me what manner you have in mind.

"As a father," he says, "through a son." You have not yet made clear what I am asking. I am not asking about the persons of the speaker and the hearer, but about how the one gives the command and how the other receives it. "The Father," they say, "commanded, and the Son worked." Show me how the Son created and how the Father commanded. "The Father," they say, "gave the command by a word, and the Son did the work." In what manner? Did he do the work by putting his hand to it? That would be a sign that he endured bodily labor. Or did he carry out some operation? "No," they say, "he himself made things by a word." See how the wickedness multiplies! Tell me the words the Father spoke, and set before me the word by which the Son made things. But I will not give you room to say whatever you like. I will lead you, whether you want it or not, into the divine teaching and show you the words of the Creator. "God said, Let there be light." "God said, Let there be a firmament." Who was it that spoke? At once they counter, "The Father spoke, and the Son carried out the command." If these were the words of someone giving a command, God would not have said, "Let there be light," but "Make the light," and the Son would have heard and made it. But come, tell me: why are the same words found in both places? "God said, Let there be light, and there was light." And again, "God said, Let there be a firmament, and there was a firmament." If the Father used the words "Let there be light" and "Let there be a firmament," why did those same words not take effect and accomplish the work? Why did they need other words? This is a serious matter. Suppose, as the heretics say, that the Father spoke, and the Son stood nearby and heard God say, "Let there be light," and then the Son took up the words and made the light. Could there be such recklessness in a raving mind as to say that the Word of God underwent bodily operation and labor? And if they still persist in speaking of some bodily operation and not of divine power, David comes forward and refutes them: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were established."

Now if the Father said, "Let there be light," and the words went out and did no work but stood waiting for the Son, was the Father lacking something? Did he make up for the lack through the Son? He said, "Let there be light," and nature did not follow. He said, "Let there be a firmament," and the word accomplished no work. The Father spoke and waited for the Son to create. See what you are doing! Perhaps while you are contriving this you are bringing in another impiety, as though the Father were weak and the Son strong.

Come, tell me the manner. What does "through the Son" mean? "Through the Son," they say, "he made the creatures." And who made the Son? "The Father made him." May Christ wipe away this terrible sin, for I tremble even to speak when I recount the blasphemy. Do not be surprised at this. When he was about to bring blasphemy into the account, he did not do so in plain words. He was cautious and did not state the blasphemy openly but covered it with a veil. So when one spoke to God himself, he said, "Come, touch his flesh, and see whether he will not bless you to your face," instead of saying "curse." The disciples of the heretics say (let this be heard as coming from them and not from us), "The Father made only the Son, and the Son made all the other creatures." Tell me how he came to be. If the Son came to be by God's will, and we and the other creatures also came to be by God's will, what lies between the worshiper and the one who receives the worship? If he came to be in the same way as I did, why does he demand worship from me? If he came from nothing by God's will, and the world came from nothing by God's will, I do not see what lies between them. Suppose God the Father made him [?], and the Son made the other creatures. If there is some distance between them through which the Son came forth, tell me. But if there is none, and the Son came to be from nothing by will alone, and all the other creatures came to be from nothing by will, how can one who came to be from nothing by God's will, as we did, receive worship from us?

"Yes," they say, "he does receive it, for he is not like the other creatures. He surpasses all creatures and every rank of things that have been made." They are clever only with words, and they insult his nature. If he is not the Creator and Lord of the creatures, and the one who brought them out of nothing, then being above the creatures does not mean he must receive worship from them. For a creature does not receive worship from creatures. The heavens are greater than the earth, but the earth does not owe worship to the heavens. The stars are greater than the plants, but the plants do not worship the stars. An angel is greater than a human being, but a human being does not worship an angel. And why speak of human nature at all? How is an ant like Gabriel, or a gnat like Michael? Yet because the one are creatures and the other are creatures, in the matter of worship the angels come down to these, and these creatures go up to them, and together they form a crown of worship around the throne. By their superiority the angels are set apart and distinct from these, but by being created and by worship they are joined and close to one another.

Listen to blessed David: "Praise the Lord from the heavens, praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his hosts. Sun and moon, all stars and light, heavens of heavens, and waters above the heavens." When he has finished listing those who are above the world, he immediately adds, "Praise the Lord from the earth." With the same words he appoints the same worship. Angels do not worship in one way and human beings in another. "Praise the Lord," he says, "from the heavens; praise the Lord from the earth. Praise him, all his angels; dragons and all deeps." How are angels like dragons? "Fire and hail, snow and ice, wind and storm, wild beasts and all cattle": bears, lions, leopards, panthers, boars and all wild beasts; and the cattle, the camel, the donkey and the ox. All of these worship together with the angels. They do not think about superiority of rank; they recognize the honor of worship, which is common to all. "Wild beasts," he says, "and all cattle, creeping things and birds": ravens praise together with angels. "Creeping things," he says: vipers, snakes, scorpions and every kind of reptile. Do you see that a higher honor does not lessen the worship of the lowlier? The angels are higher creatures, but that does not mean the others have no share in worship. Rather, the honor of the Lord and the divine essence are to be glorified by all, for all creatures owe worship to the Creator. But now show me the difference that lies between. When you speak of the Father and say that all things are from him, your very expression, even without words, shows that you think him superior. Even before they speak, the heretics blaspheme with their faces. When they dispute about the Father, they begin by saying, "One God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things." Your face blasphemes before your tongue does; your expression belittles him before your words do. O what contempt! The prophets magnify even the creatures, and the heretics belittle the Creator. David honors and magnifies the creatures: "How great are your works, O Lord!" The godly magnify even the works, and the impious belittle the Creator.

They say that the prophets magnify created things because these do not have greatness of themselves. The Son, however, should not be magnified beyond what he is, they say, or have his honour raised past some measure. They talk as though they had the authority to show mercy and kindness to the Son. Their words are impious, and they are impious because they do not understand the meaning of the words. I know Christ as magnified, not by any addition to his nature, but through the gratitude of those who worship him. Listen to blessed David, who magnifies him: “I will praise the name of my God with a song,” he says, “and I will magnify him with praise.” He does not magnify him from smallness. Rather, he magnifies the Benefactor whom unbelievers thought small: “I will make him great with thanksgiving.” Paul magnifies the Life-giver: “Whether by life or by death, Christ will be magnified in my body.” Why does he magnify him? Because he cannot find the measure. Why would he magnify him? Because a human tongue cannot reach that honour. He magnifies not the nature of the one who is glorified, but the words of the praises. I magnify Christ as far as I am able, but not as though I could speak in keeping with his greatness.

Just as the godly magnify God, so also they exalt him: “I will exalt you, my God and my King.” Do they then raise him from lowliness to height? What, then, does “I will exalt” mean? It is another way of saying, “I will proclaim your exaltedness.” And since human nature is not enough for this, the divine Scriptures command, “Exalt the Lord our God,” for he is above even exaltedness, and his height is beyond the measure of your glorifying. That is why the three youths, schooled in understanding, did as they did. They made the furnace into a church and by the power of faith turned the flame into dew. They blessed as far as they were able and left aside what was beyond their ability: “Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord,” they say, “bless him and exalt him above all forever.” They did not consider it enough to exalt the Exalted One, but went on to exalt him still more, for they saw human weakness put to shame by his surpassing greatness. And here the three youths, taking a certain care, summon all creatures to worship. They mentioned angels and archangels, the powers, the waters, the sun and the moon, rivers and springs, the earth and its fruits, the sea and its great sea creatures, birds and cattle, wild beasts and creeping things, and human beings. In all this they made no mention of the Son, nor even a hint of the Holy Spirit, for the Son is not in the rank of those who worship, but of the one who receives worship.

But perhaps someone will ask how the three youths could have brought the Son into their call to worship, when they did not even know that he is the Son. They were not aware of it, for the prophets said nothing openly about the honour of the Son. But the name of the Holy Spirit was proclaimed through the prophets. Although the name of the Son seemed something unfamiliar to the youths, the Spirit's name lay plainly before them. Isaiah says, “They rebelled and provoked his Holy Spirit,” and blessed David says, “Do not cast me away from your presence, O Lord, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.” See how firm this is. David and Isaiah did not come after the three youths, so no one can say that this was not known at that time and was only revealed later. The three youths came after David and Isaiah, so they were acquainted with the writings of the prophets and knew that the Holy Spirit had been proclaimed. Why, then, do they bring all those creatures to worship and not mention the Spirit? They name angels, archangels, powers and the rest one by one, yet they did not mention the Spirit. It is because they saw him not yoked together with the creatures, but revealed as from God. They themselves had been enlightened by the Holy Spirit, and, strengthened by the power of the Holy Spirit, they trampled on the fire. Iron that is refined into steel and quenched becomes harder and sharper. In the same way, when the souls of the righteous are tempered by the Holy Spirit, they count fire as nothing, and water, heaven, earth and everything in between as well.

But so that I may bring the argument to this point, and so that the disciples of the heretics may not think it an empty opinion, I will bring in the words of Paul. He lists the things the Saviour created, a passage the heretics twist. They have turned the phrase “it came to be through him” upside down so as to show by it that the Son is somehow lesser. But in another place Paul does not say “through him,” but “by him”: “By him,” he says, “all things were established, whatever is in heaven and whatever is on earth.” Pay careful attention to “whatever is in heaven and whatever is on earth.” He lists the creatures so as not to lead us into some false opinion or needless stumbling, and so as to keep the uncreated nature free of stain. “All things,” he says, “came to be through him, whether thrones or dominions or authorities.” And again: “By him all things were established.” Which “all things”? Thrones, authorities, dominions, principalities: all things were established through him and for him. And not only “through him” and “for him,” but “by him” and “for him.” “And he is before all things, and by him all things were established.”

Why did he leave out the other creatures and not say “whether sun or moon, whether heaven or earth, whether stars or anything else”? The visible things are plainly known to belong to the rank of creatures, so he leaves out what is obvious. Among the invisible things, however, there are the ranks of those who worship and also the uncreated nature that receives worship. So he thinks it necessary to list everything that is above the heavens, to free the Holy Spirit from blasphemy and to give the heretics no cause for rejoicing. “All things,” he says, “came to be through him, whether thrones, principalities, authorities or dominions.” And he did not say “the Holy Spirit.”

Now let them tell us how the heretics arrived at this. They did not hesitate to pour out blasphemy against our weakness and to fill every city with it, as though the Church proclaimed three almighty ones. But I would like to persuade them once more not to blame us, but the prophets. If I were putting forward words of my own devising and inventing novelties against the truth, they would be right to slander us. But if we are repeating the words of the prophets, the accusation falls not on us who interpret them, but on those who laid down our religion. We have spoken, not in the way they slandered us, but as we believe. The Church does not acknowledge three almighty ones, but one power that holds all things. In truth, almightiness is recognized in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Whoever speaks of three gods separate from one another, let him be anathema. And whoever does not confess the Trinity as one Almighty, let him be anathema.

But do not think these words strange or new when you see the truth being slandered as blasphemy. Call to mind the first saints. Stephen saw the heavens opened and the Saviour at the right hand of God. He proclaimed what he saw and was suspected of blasphemy because of it. When that holy and loud trumpet sounded, “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God,” the Jews could not endure the truth. They stopped their ears, as though blasphemy were being spoken and not truth proclaimed. So do not think it new or strange if the true word is taken for blasphemy, for wickedness is in the habit of casting its own faults onto the virtuous. If we have made some presumptuous claim, we will be judged for the presumption. If we have invented some novelty, we will give account for the innovation. But if it is the words of the prophets that are being recounted, what fault is that of ours? “Thus says the Lord Almighty: Behold, I will come and dwell in your midst, says the Lord, and many nations will take refuge in you, and you will know that the Lord Almighty has sent me.”

Why do you pick at our words and not at those of the prophets? Those who have the truth are bold to give their verdict. Where there is truth, there is no fear at all. Where there is faith, there is no room for shrinking back. Where there is faith, there is strength, and where there is unbelief, there is timidity. The Life-giver said to the disciples, “Why are you fainthearted? Do you have no faith?” Do you see? Where there is unbelief, there is faintheartedness, and where there is faith, there is strength. Scripture says, “Stephen, full of faith and power, did great signs among the people.” And Paul says of Abraham that he did not waver in unbelief but was strengthened in faith. I too am bold to say that whatever name belongs to the Father belongs also to the Son. “Blessed,” it says, “is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” And the Life-giver says, “I have come in my Father's name.” Let us ask, then, what the Father's name is. The Scriptures proclaim the Father's name as “God” and “Lord”: “This is my name.” Pay careful attention: “I am the Lord God,” he says, “this is my name.” If “Lord” and “God” is the Father's name, and I find the same name given to the Son, is it not plain that the Son is Lord and God? “Blessed,” it says, “is he who comes in the name of the Lord. The Lord our God has appeared to us. Blessed is he who has come in the name of the Lord.” That is why blessed Thomas, who received proof of the resurrection itself, saw that whatever name belongs to the Father belongs also to the Son, and cried out loudly, “My Lord and my God!”

Let us see whether God has any other name, and whether the Son does not share in it too. “Let them know,” it says, “that your name is Lord.” But when I say “share,” I do not mean by grace, but by sharing the same nature. David says, “Let them know that your name is Lord, and that you alone are Most High over all the earth.” And the apostle says, “For us there is one Lord, Jesus Christ.” “One” and “alone” have the same force. The heretic gives the name “God” to the Father and “Lord” to the Son. Since you have given “Lord” to the Son, and the prophet says, “Let them know that your name is Lord, and that you alone are Most High over all the earth,” would you dare to say that there is one Lord and that Jesus alone is Most High, and not the Father? Think about it. How would you dare to say that Jesus is the one Lord when you hear from the prophet, “Your name is Lord, and you alone are Most High”? If you take that to refer only to the Father, could you deny that Jesus is Lord? And if, on the other hand, you take it to refer to the Son, could you really think that the Father is not Lord? Far from it! May it never be! Rather, let your words agree with your mind. Do not call him Lord with your words while regarding him as a servant in your mind.

Would you call the Father Lord? “Yes,” he says. Would you call the Son Lord as well? “Yes,” he says. Then how is it that you say “alone Lord and Most High” in the one place and “one Lord” in the other? From here on we must not reason it out, but believe. If I say God the Father, God the Son and God the Holy Spirit, you call me a believer in three gods. And if he says that the Father is Lord and the Son is Lord, what shall we call him? A believer in two lords, perhaps? Think about it. You dare to say there are two lords. Even if you do not say it in words, you hold it in your mind, for you speak of one lordship of the Father and another lordship of the Son: one an unrestricted authority, the other subject to the lordship of the Father. If that is so, then there is no longer one Lord, nor one honour and nature of lordship. Both cannot be called one Lord if the Father is Lord in one way and the Son is Lord in another. I am amazed at how you can serve a divided lordship, when the Lord himself says, “You cannot serve two masters.” But let us go on to what lies ahead. The Father is Lord and God, and the Son is Lord and God, as has already been shown: “Let them know that your name is Lord,” and “there is one Lord, Jesus Christ.” Let us see whether we find any other name of God in the Scriptures.

Blessed Moses says, “If the children of Israel ask me, ‘What is the name of the one who sent you?’ what shall I say?” Here too, notice “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Pay attention to how he gives the true signs: “Say, ‘He Who Is has sent me.’” If so, the Father's name is “He Who Is.” Let us see whether the Son does not have the same name as well, or else our defence is in vain. “He Who Is,” he says, “has sent me.” What do you say to the apostle? “By ‘He Who Is,’ am I to understand the Father or the Son?” You are full of great folly when you ask, “The Father or the Son?” You divide the honour and fail to recognize their partnership in equal honour. Whom would you call “He Who Is”? The one of whom the Scripture spoke and whom I proclaimed. Moses speaks of “He Who Is” with reference to the Father, and I speak of “He Who Is” with reference to the Son: “I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites. To them belong the adoption, the giving of the law, the worship, the covenants and the promises. Theirs are the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, comes Christ, He Who Is over all, God blessed forever.” Do you see that the name of the Father and the name of the Son agree with each other in word and in fact? “He Who Is has sent me.” “He Who Is over all, God blessed forever.” Is the word somehow forced? Does it not bear witness in very fact? Why do you accuse our tongue and despise the words of the prophets?

Let us look at yet another name. The words “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” were not spoken in vain: every name that belongs to the Father belongs also to the Son. Blessed Isaiah says to the people, “You have forsaken the Lord God your Saviour, and you did not remember the Lord your Helper. Therefore you will plant an unfaithful plant and unfaithful seed, because you forsook God your Saviour.” God's name is Saviour, and God's name is Helper. Now let us see whether the Son is not also Saviour. Listen to the angels who sang praises and brought the good news to the shepherds: “We bring you good news of great joy,” they say, “for to you is born this day a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord.” “You have forsaken,” it says, “God your Saviour, and you did not remember the Lord your Helper.” And where would you find the Son called Helper? A man came and brought him his son, who was possessed by a demon, and said, “Good Teacher, I brought my son to your disciples, and they could not heal him.” And the Saviour asks, “How long has it been?” He asked not so that he himself might learn, but so that those standing nearby might learn how many years of illness he was clearing away, and might benefit. “Since childhood,” the man says. “It has often thrown him into fire and into water. I told your disciples, and they could not heal him. But if you can do anything, help us.” Pay careful attention. The Saviour accepted his coming, but rejected the doubting mind in which he came. If someone says to God, “If you can do anything,” that is not fitting for God. The other saying is fitting: “All things are possible.” The man approached him as he would a prophet or an apostle, who has only a limited power, so that there are some things he can do and some he cannot. So the Saviour mocks his ignorance, or rather instructs his foolish mind, because he had said, “If you can.” And by keeping silent he rebukes his insolence. “All things,” he says, “are possible to the one who believes.” He makes nothing plain in words, but the man standing near him perceived his displeasure from his face. When the man who had erred saw that the Life-giver was reproving him and showing his displeasure by his face, how he cried out! “I believe, Lord,” he says, “help my unbelief!” It was another way of saying, “I have erred. I did not know your power. Make up what I lack; help my unbelief.” For it was unbelief to say, “If you can, help.” The demoniac's father repented, but the deluded heretics, who often call upon the Son in their prayers, do not repent.

O what folly! Suppose you do not regard the Son as equal in honour with God, nor the Spirit of the Son. Will you not even make him equal in honour with the prophets? Have you not heard the words of the prophet Elijah: “If I am a man of God,” he says, “let fire come down and consume your captain of fifty and your fifty men”? The prophet commands with authority, and is the Lord of the prophets to offer prayers? Elijah commands with authority creatures he was not lord over, because his godliness gave him boldness. There one could see a man of flesh giving orders to the lightning's fire and bringing fire down on his adversaries. And elsewhere the same blessed Elijah says to his disciple, “Ask something of me before I am taken up from you, and I will do it for you.” He did not say, “I will intercede,” but “I will do it,” before he was taken up. The prophets command with authority by the power of their faith, and do you summon the Lord of the prophets to subjection and count yourself a sharer in his prayers? Does Joshua, the Lord's namesake, not put you to shame? He made the sun stand still without prayer. Did he say to the Lord, “Make the sun stand still”? No, he said with authority, “Let the sun stand still!” The servant had that much power, or rather the name did, since it was the Lord's own name. The sun stood in awe not of him, but of the royal name. And would the Truth himself not do good with authority, but merely act as an intercessor? But let us go on to what lies ahead.

The Father's name is “He Who Is,” and the Son's name is “He Who Is.” The Father's name is Helper, and the Son's name is Helper. The Father's name is Almighty, and the Son's name is Almighty. If I were saying this by issuing a verdict of my own, do not accept it. But if I say it by demonstration, do not deny it. Consider what will happen to you if you deny what I say. You insult the prophets, and if you insult the prophets, you deny God, and going further still you fall into impiety. If you regard as mine the words the prophets spoke, you insult not me, who interpret them, but the voices of the prophets and the inspiration of God. Do you not know that God counts insults to the prophets as his own? When Samuel was rejected by the people, what did God say? “They have not rejected you,” he says, “but me.” And to make it plain that whoever does not listen to a teacher and a prophet does not listen [to God] [?], he says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, go to the house of the rebellious and speak to them, and they will not listen to you, for they are not willing to listen to me.” If they listen to you, they listen to me as well, and if to me, then to you also.

It has already been shown that the Son is called Almighty, but another prophet also bears witness: “He who builds his ascent in the heavens and establishes his promise on the earth, the Lord Almighty is his name.” Who is it that built the ascent in the heavens and established the promise on earth, if not the one who said to the disciples as he was taken up, “I am with you until the end of the world”? Then there is: “Behold, I will come,” says the Lord Almighty, “and dwell in your midst.” What does “I will dwell” mean? The evangelist explains: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” “And many nations will take refuge in the Lord, and you will know that the Lord Almighty has sent me.” “Where is it written,” they ask, “that the Son is Almighty?” Where is it written that the Father is Almighty? You demand words, and I demand words. You gather forces, and I muster forces. He spoke through the prophets, so receive it from the prophets. “Search the Scriptures,” says the Saviour. No one searches what is obvious, only what is hidden. “Search the Scriptures,” he says.

See how the Trinity is proclaimed under the form of one authority. Listen to God, who says, “Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead the people astray.” Pay careful attention: “who bite the preaching with their teeth [?] and speak peace with their mouths, but peace was not given in their mouths. For there is no one who will listen to the false prophets. But I,” he says, “will be filled, I will be filled with power by the Spirit of the Lord.” Either accept this and believe it, or erase it from your mind, for you cannot erase the living Scriptures. “For there is no one,” he says, “who will listen to false prophets, but I will be filled with power by the Spirit of the Lord.” He cannot say, “by my own Spirit,” but says, “I will be filled with power by the Spirit of the Lord.” Who is speaking here? Explain these words to me, so that I may understand the meaning of this power. And in another place God says, “I will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel, but will stand against them in opposition. But I will have mercy on the children of Judah, and I will save them by the Lord their God.” Will you not save them by yourself, then, but by another God? The heretics do not understand that the words of the prophets are veiled [?]. If prophecy proclaimed things openly, it would not be prophecy, but preaching; not prophecy, but gospel. What is plain is gospel, and what is obscured is prophecy. “And you, Daniel,” it says, “seal the words of this vision.” It is another way of saying, “Cover them in obscurity.” He does not mean “Hide the book,” which people read to this day, but the meaning of the words. The words of the prophets were sealed, and they are explained by the Gospel.

Again God says to the people, “What shall I do with you? You did not accept correction. I cut down your prophets with the sword of my mouth, and even so you did not listen to me. I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.” Why does he not say, “as I overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah,” but “as God overthrew”? Did you liken yourself to someone else? [?] “I overthrew you,” he says, “as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and even so you did not believe me.” Do you see the power hidden here, or rather brought openly to light? Do you see the power of godliness made bold? Why, then, would you blame someone who calls the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit Almighty? When I say God and God and God, I do not mean three gods, but one. In the same way, when I say Almighty and Almighty and Almighty, I do not mean three almighty ones, but one. Let the Saviour's words put you to shame, which he spoke to the Jews: “In your law it is written that the testimony of two men is true. When it says God and God, do you not believe?” [?] But even though he says, “I and the Father,” he does not mean two gods separate from one another, but one Godhead, his own and the Father's. He makes this plain with the rest of the saying: “I and my Father are one.” He says “one” because they are inseparable, and “are” so that no one may think the persons have no real existence of their own.

Let us take care and be watchful [?] in our souls. Cast off the poison, wipe away the rust, scrape off the tarnish, and be obedient to God, to whom even demons were obedient. Let your changes of conduct put you to shame. Do not be a believer in church and then become a heretic once you have gone out. Do not revere the word here and then slide into brutishness once you have gone out. A fickle soul does not stand firm amid changes [?] and never becomes steadfast. A God-fearing soul passes through changes but is not itself changed. The godly person is godly even in war, a brave contender in famine, and not made slack by plenty. The godly person is self-controlled and patient in all things and does not change as circumstances change. The soul of the righteous is neither shaken by the turmoil of war nor made slack by the comforts of ease. When right glory is proclaimed, it is found to be an eager listener, and toward the perverse it is quick to resist [?]. It does not break away from unity, and it is not double-minded.

The Lord God is one; come, let us follow him. But if you follow error, you will end in error. A fine wine is not harmed by being moved: even if you pour it from vessel to vessel, it keeps the same taste and the same quality, while a poor wine is quickly shown up by being moved. In the same way the soul of the God-fearing is not defeated by changes but overcomes them, while the shallower soul is quickly shown up. These are not my words but those of the blessed prophet Jeremiah, who thundered against the nation of the Moabites. For a time they lived at ease and thought they would always enjoy their ease, and they trampled on Jerusalem in her captivity. So the prophet rebukes them: “Do not boast of your ease, and do not grow proud of your success, for you have not yet been changed; your change will come too.” He had not yet put them to the test, so that their wills might be revealed. And what does he say? “Moab has been at ease from his youth, and has never known a change into hard times. Moab has been at ease from his youth and has prided himself on his glory; he has never been poured from vessel to vessel”—which is to say, he has never gone into captivity—“therefore his taste has remained in him, and his scent is unchanged.” Brothers, we must also bring forward this example from the divine teaching of the sealed holy Scriptures. Why compare divine things to wine? Because the prophet's teaching is sure salvation. “Moab,” he says, “has been at ease from his youth and has prided himself on his glory; he has not been poured from vessel to vessel, he has never gone into captivity; therefore his taste has remained in him, and his scent is unchanged.” The Church has been tried by evil and poured from vessel to vessel, from peace into war and from war into peace, and its sweet fragrance has remained in it. “We are a sweet fragrance,” it says, “in Christ.”

I have said all this, and I know that I have spoken at length. But since I had been slandered, I had to show that my cause was just. For a slander of this kind has spread through all the churches: the claim is not that one person spoke wrongly, but that everyone is [?]. I have given an answer for myself and for the whole Church: the Church has one Lord and one God, one Creator, one Almighty and one King. But when you hear “one,” think of the inseparable Trinity as God, the endless and incorruptible kingdom, the glory and the truth. It is never divided, but abides and remains eternal and life-giving. May it be granted to all of us to enjoy it truly, and to give glory to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
